title: Copying another's manner
core: All four describe reproducing something that belongs to someone else — a manner, a voice, a face, a style. They split on three axes: **what** is copied (a person's tics, a person's excellence, an artist's style), **how faithfully** (exact, inflated, loose homage), and **why** (to reach that level, to get a laugh, to attack, to pay tribute). The copy itself is never the issue on the GRE; the attitude behind it is.

words.nuance: The only one aimed at the copier's own improvement rather than at an audience: you take the model as a standard and try to reach or beat it. Nothing is put on display, and the thing copied is the achievement, not the mannerisms — you emulate a champion's discipline, you don't emulate his limp.

Live, close-range reproduction of surface behaviour — the vowel, the gait, the throat-clearing — performed at the person, usually in front of others. Fidelity is the whole point, which is exactly what makes it cruel; the technical uses (a hoverfly **mimics** a wasp) keep the exactness and drop the malice.

The only one that is deliberately *un*faithful: it picks one real feature and inflates it, so the distortion is the method, not a failure. Figuratively it's a charge you level at an opponent — "a caricature of my position" accuses him of arguing against the inflated version.

Operates on a style or genre across a whole work, not on a person's face or habits, and openly announces what it's borrowing. No mockery (that's parody), no concealment (that's plagiarism), no ambition to surpass — which is why "mere pastiche" is the insult: competent borrowed manner with nothing of the author's own.

exam_note: The trap is connotation: **emulate** is the positive one and is often the answer where a sentence praises a successor, while **caricature** and **mimic** are offered as neutral-looking synonyms of "imitate" that quietly import ridicule.
